strengths: Large scale: 21k+ hours of raw video curated down to 7,089 hours (2.7M clips) with a further balanced 1,146-hour HQ subset, representing one of the largest dynamic real-world video datasets with per-frame camera pose and depth annotations reported to date.

Comprehensive multi-modal annotation pipeline combining geometric information (camera poses, depth maps via an enhanced MegaSaM+UniDepthv2/DepthAnythingv2 pipeline, dynamic masks via SAM2) with rich structured semantic captions (scene description, camera description, category tags, shot summary) and derived cinematographic motion instructions.

Reasonably justified choice of pose/depth estimator: the paper empirically compares MegaSaM against COLMAP, DROID-SLAM, Fast3R, MonST3R, and VGGT and explains the accuracy/speed trade-offs that motivated the selection.

Thoughtful quality-control pipeline with multiple filtering criteria (aesthetics, luminance, OCR, motion/VMAF) and novel trajectory-based metrics (MoveDist, RotAngle, TrajTurns) to characterize and filter camera motion quality.
Useful comparison against Panda-70M processed through the same pipeline, showing SpatialVID/HQ has substantially richer camera motion diversity and better video quality distributions.

The 'spatial enhancement' captioning strategy, which fuses VLM-derived descriptions with camera-pose priors via an LLM, is a sensible and illustrative idea for correcting VLM's frequent misjudgment of motion direction (Fig. 9).

Extensive statistical/qualitative analysis (scene tag sunburst, word clouds, caption length distributions, motion-direction donut charts) gives a fairly transparent picture of dataset composition and coverage.
weaknesses: No downstream experiments demonstrating that models trained on SpatialVID actually improve camera-controlled video generation, dynamic 3D reconstruction, or world-model tasks; the abstract's claim that the dataset 'directly foster[s] improved model generalization and performance' is not empirically substantiated anywhere in the manuscript, which is a significant gap for a dataset intended to enable exactly these downstream applications.

The camera poses and depth are pseudo-labels from an automatic SLAM/MVS pipeline (MegaSaM), not verified ground truth; validation is limited to qualitative trajectory visualizations on a handful of examples (Fig. 6) and an 'acceleration plausibility' heuristic, with no quantitative benchmarking against known ground-truth trajectories (e.g., on established pose-estimation benchmarks) to establish annotation accuracy at scale.

Caption quality (from Gemini + Qwen3) is assessed only qualitatively via a few illustrative examples; there is no human evaluation, no quantitative caption-accuracy metric, and no error analysis of hallucination rates or the frequency of residual motion-direction mistakes after the 'spatial enhancement' step.

The initial video collection relies on manual screening of ~33k YouTube videos by human curators, which is labor-intensive, difficult to reproduce, and not fully quantified (no discussion of annotator agreement, screening criteria consistency, or scalability of this manual step for future dataset extension).

Potential dataset bias: video categories are dominated by a few types (walk, house tour, drive), and although the HQ subset attempts rebalancing, the underlying diversity of scene content (e.g., few indoor scenes beyond house tours, limited representation of certain geographic/cultural settings) is not deeply analyzed.

No discussion of licensing, copyright, or ethical/privacy considerations around large-scale scraping and redistribution of YouTube videos (e.g., depicting identifiable people), which is an increasingly important consideration for dataset papers at this scale.

Known failure modes of MegaSaM (dominant moving foreground objects, collinear camera/object motion, lack of support for variable focal length or strong radial distortion) are acknowledged but not quantified in terms of what fraction of the final released clips may still be affected, leaving residual annotation-quality uncertainty for downstream users.
